newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Feature - No dissent as Dutch race towards EMU.
newsitem.headline: Feature - No dissent as Dutch race towards EMU.

text.p: While several of its European Union partners are racked by division over the issue, the Netherlands is racing wholeheartedly towards a single European currency, the final stage of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU).

Opinion polls show the Dutch are strongly in favour of EMU, despite the ultimate abolition of the guilder -- their beloved currency for the last three centuries -- in favour of the new currency, the euro.

Eurosceptics, cynics who eschew a federalist approach to Europe by citing national sovereignty issues, are hard to find in this small trading nation, which has been a prime beneficiary of the removal of trading barriers in Europe.

The Netherlands serves as an economic model for neighbouring countries aspiring to qualify for EMU, according to economists who point to the strong currency, low inflation and interest rates, steady economic growth and falling unemployment.
These achievements are seen as products of measures introduced over the last 15 years to make the country more competitive and forge a close link between the Dutch and German currencies.
LITTLE OPPOSITION TO EMU IN NETHERLANDS
Opposition, where it does exist, comes from politicians more concerned about the terms under which other weaker countries will join a single currency rather than the euro itself.
Political analysts cite the Netherlands' long history of support for European integration in explaining the lack of opposition to EMU.

"Most Dutch would argue that European integration is in the Dutch interest," said Dr Jan Rood, deputy director of studies at the Clingendael Institute for International Relations, an independent research and training foundation in The Hague.

"We have always profited from the (European) agricultural policies, which were favourable to the Dutch. The Netherlands is export-oriented. We're very interested in opening up European markets," he added.
MORE ECONOMIC INFLUENCE THROUGH EMU
Rood said the Netherlands now had no influence over monetary policy and little influence over economic policy, independent of Germany, because of the close ties between the two countries.
This meant the Dutch would have a greater input into the operation of their economy under a single currency as they would have a seat on the board of the new European central bank.
Dutch central bank chief Wim Duisenberg will be the next president of the European Monetary Institute, the forerunner of the European Central Bank.

"The Dutch, in the end, have very little choice if the Germans and the French have EMU. We have only one option and that is to follow them. There's a feeling that the risks are worth taking," he said.

The main political opposition to EMU has come from the conservative Liberals (VVD), a right-leaning partner in the Netherlands three-party ruling coalition, which has threatened strong protests if EMU's convergence terms are relaxed.

Dr Hans Hoogervorst, the VVD's finance spokesman, said his party saw benefits from a single currency but it also wanted to ensure the convergence criteria for determining which countries participated were strictly adhered to.

"There's very clear gains to be be made. But unfortunately most politicians in this country are likely to agree with anything that the French and Germans decide. My party will create a big stink if the criteria are not met."
DUTCH PUBLIC SUPPORT EMU
But the VVD's concern is not shared by most Dutch people, according to a survey by the Dutch central bank, the Nederlandsche Bank, in January and February this year.
It found that 70 percent of people and 80 percent of companies considered the euro to be as acceptable as the guilder.

"Interest in the euro and in EMU has shown a distinct increase, and nearly one-half of private persons and enterprises hold that they are sufficiently informed," the central bank said in its March 1996 quarterly bulletin.

Professor Andre Szasz, a former central bank board member, said the EMU debate was less controversial in the Netherlands because people had fewer illusions about their economic autonomy in Europe than some of their neighbours.
"We are a very open economy. There's no way we could pursue an independent monetary policy and accept whatever follows for the exchange rate," he said.
ECONOMICS THE REAL ISSUE

Professor Paul Verhaegen, director of economic affairs at the country's major employer body, Confederation of Netherlands Industry, noted that while EMU had emerged as a contentious political debate in some European countries, it was seen more in economic terms in the Netherlands.
It will cost the country an estimated 7.5 billion guilders in total but will also cut transaction, administration and other costs by two billion guilders per year.

The Netherlands is now one of the few EU members with a deficit to GDP ratio below the three percent limit set for EMU, although its debt to GDP ratio is still much too high at 78.8 percent compared with the required 60 percent.
"In four years you get your money back," said Verhaegen who, like many people in the Netherlands, believes that on this basis, it makes good sense.
